description: Solo participant from Dnipro building an interactive Space Mission Design Game: players design, launch and operate a space mission while balancing budget, mass, power, communications and orbital constraints.
summary: Trade Space is a browser game in which the player designs, launches and operates a complete space mission. Every choice (orbit, instruments, spacecraft bus, solar arrays, battery, pointing control, communications, computer, launch vehicle, lifetime) spends mass, power, money, data or time, and six live resource bars show the effect at once. The mission is then flown in 3D: a launch sequence with telemetry, a true-scale orbit over real NASA imagery, shadow, ground track and downlink. A mission report explains what cost the player science and why, and a risk analysis flies the same design 600 times to show how likely it is to succeed. The game addresses the challenge by turning abstract trade-offs into decisions with visible consequences. It includes a ten-lesson guided first mission, a career mode, team play with four roles, and case files based on real NASA missions. It runs in English and Ukrainian, with no installation or account.
details: What it does. The player takes a mission objective (monitor wildfires from Earth orbit, map water ice at the Moon's south pole, or forecast dust storms at Mars) and builds a spacecraft in ten steps: orbit, instruments, bus, solar arrays, battery, pointing control, communications, computer, launch vehicle and lifetime. Six resources are always visible: mass against the rocket's limit, power against what the arrays supply, budget, data produced against data returned, schedule and forecast science. A design review explains every problem in plain language. Each part has a detail card that explains how the real hardware works and where it has flown. How it works. The model is simple and explained inside the game. Power is averaged over a full orbit, shadow included. Propellant is sized from dry mass and the chosen orbit. Launch capacity shrinks with destination. Data above the daily link capacity is lost. A seeded simulation flies the mission year by year with random launch failures, solar storms, hardware faults and dust storms. The same simulation runs 600 times for the risk analysis. What the player sees. A 3D spacecraft assembled from the chosen parts; a launch sequence that explains the gravity turn and staging; orbits drawn to true scale over NASA imagery with real periods and speeds; the planet rotating under the orbit so a ground track builds up; instruments switching off in shadow when the battery is too small. The report gives a score, the causes of lost science, simulated data products for each instrument and a note on how NASA solved the same problem. Ways to play. A ten-lesson guided first mission; a career with contracts for Earth, the Moon and Mars; case files that share a weakness with Kepler, Opportunity and Galileo; single missions on three difficulty levels; a team mode with four roles and a go / no-go poll; a trade study table to compare designs. Impact. Students usually learn orbits, power and communications as separate topics. Trade Space lets them practise the mission-level decision, see why a design fails and try again in minutes. Limits. Masses, power figures and costs are rounded teaching values, not engineering data. Data products are simulated on top of real NASA maps and labelled as such. Team mode is played on one screen. Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page; three.js for 3D. The code, the in-game texts, the Ukrainian translation and the demo slides were generated with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), directed and tested by the team; this is stated in the game footer and in the page metadata.
